verses.translation_literal: A prayer of Moses, the man of God. Lord, a dwelling [place] you [yourself] have been for us in generation and generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: A prayer, and its author named: Moses, the man of God. He does not begin with a request. He begins with an address, low and steady: Lord. You have been our home. Not a house of stone, not a tent that the wind can lift, but you, from one generation to the next, and the next, and the next.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice is plural: 'for us'. Moses speaks for a people who have no land of their own yet and have been in tents, so 'dwelling' (ma'on) is the weightiest word he could pick. Ibn Ezra reasons from the plural that this psalm is Moses' own and not David's, and that the line echoes Deuteronomy 33:27. The opening word is 'Adonai', and the Hebrew sets 'you' (atah) in front of the verb, so the sentence leans on you, not on any other shelter. The KJV smooths 'in generation and generation' into 'in all generations', which loses the repeated word, the way a drum beat repeats. It also prints the title as a separate 'verse 0', so the KJV numbers are one off for the whole psalm in the first verse. 'Man of God' (ish ha-elohim) is Radak's 'prophet'; in the ancient world it names someone sent and spoken to by the deity, not a saint.

philological_notes.note: A dwelling or refuge, an abode, used elsewhere of God's heavenly residence ('from your holy habitation', Deuteronomy 26:15). Rashi reads 'a dwelling and a place to flee to'; Radak 'a place and a shelter'; Metzudat David compares it to a house that guards from flood and rain.
Literally 'in generation and generation', a repetition that means 'every generation, without end'. English translations usually flatten it to 'all generations'.

verses.translation_literal: Before mountains were born, and you writhed [in labor with] earth and world, and from age to age, you [are] God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before the mountains were born, before you laboured and the earth and the inhabited world came out of you, before there was any age to measure by, even then, and on to the last age: you are God.
verses.directors_commentary: This is birth language, and the translators hide it. The mountains 'were born' (yulladu), and God 'brought forth' the earth with the verb chol, which is the verb of labor pains (it is the verb in Metzudat Zion's cross-reference to Psalm 51, 'in iniquity I was brought forth', hololti). The KJV's 'formed' is a potter's verb and misses the picture: the earth is a child God bore. The mountains are named because, as Ibn Ezra says, they seem the oldest things there are ('the hills of antiquity'), and God predates them. Note that the last word is 'El', God as power; Ibn Ezra reads it as a plain title, Radak glosses it 'able, mighty'. 'Erets' and 'tevel' together are not just a doublet: Metzudat Zion and Meiri report that some read them as wild earth and settled world. 'Olam' means a very long time out of sight, not an abstract 'eternity'; KJV's 'everlasting to everlasting' is a Latin-flavoured rendering of 'from olam to olam'.

philological_notes.note: To writhe, to be in labor, and so to bring forth. Said of God, it makes the earth a birth. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'creation' and compares Psalm 51.
Earth and the inhabited world. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion report that when they stand together, 'tevel' means the settled part and 'erets' the unsettled.

verses.translation_literal: You return man unto crushed [thing], and you said: Return, sons of man.
verses.translation_dramatic: You turn mortal man back until he is ground fine, crushed to powder under the weight of his years, and then your voice comes, low and certain: Turn back, children of Adam. Turn back.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm moves from God's age without beginning (verse 2) to the human span, and the hinge is one verb used twice: tashev, 'you return', then shuvu, 'return'. Both come from the root shuv, and the sound play is the point. God makes man shuv, and God says shuv. Give the two words the same weight and let the audience hear the echo. The second is no longer the same act as the first.

The Hebrew dakka' is a rare word for something crushed, pounded fine, from the root dk' 'to crush' (the same root as 'a crushed spirit'). The KJV's 'destruction' is a loose paraphrase that turns a physical image (grain ground in a mill, a body worn down) into an abstract fate. YLT's 'a bruised thing' is closer. The verse does not name dust, but the ancient hearer, who knew Genesis 3:19 'to dust you shall return', would have heard it. The traditional commentators read the verse in two ways. Ibn Ezra takes 'Return, sons of man' as God's command to go back to the dust from which they were taken, and Meiri likewise understands it as a decree that humans return to their dust, with old age and affliction as the messengers of death. Radak, Rashi and Metzudat David instead take shuvu as a call to repentance, spoken through the suffering that crushes a person. Malbim hears a return to the source of their dwelling in God. Hebrew shuvu, like the KJV's 'return' (and YLT's 'turn back'), can carry both senses, going back and turning back, and the KJV keeps the ambiguity without choosing. Do not play only one sense: the actor can let the command sound first like a verdict and then, on the repeat, like an invitation.

The verb forms differ: tashev is an imperfect ('you return', as a standing habit), while vattomer is the narrative form 'and you said', which sounds like a single past utterance, God's pronouncement, still in force. Bene-adam, 'sons of man', is the plain word for people as mortals, not a title. This is the psalm's first note of lament, set against the God who is 'from age to age' in verse 2.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun from the root 'to crush': something pounded or ground fine, hence 'crushed state'. It is not the ordinary word for dust ('afar). The KJV's 'destruction' abstracts it; whether it also evokes 'dust' (as Ibn Ezra and Meiri read the verse) is a matter of interpretation, not of the word itself.

The same root twice in one line: first the hiphil 'you cause to return', then the qal imperative 'return'. The root covers physical return and moral turning back (repentance). The commentators split along that line, and the verse keeps both open.

verses.translation_literal: For a thousand years in your eyes [are] like a day of yesterday when it passes, and a watch in the night.
verses.translation_dramatic: For a thousand years, seen through your eyes, are no more than yesterday: a day that has already slipped past. A thousand years, and no more than the single watch a sentry keeps in the dark.
verses.directors_commentary: The ancient night was divided into watches, three in the older Israelite reckoning (Metzudat Zion says 'a third of the night'), roughly four hours each; a sentry stood one and was relieved. That is a short, unremarkable stretch, and it is the measure of a thousand years. 'In your eyes' matters: this is God's view, not ours. The KJV 'are but as yesterday when it is past' puts 'but' in, which Hebrew doesn't, and slightly moralises. The Hebrew 'ki ya'avor' can attach to either clause; read it as 'when it passes', as the KJV does, and the day is already gone, finished, no longer felt. The KJV is faithful here, which is notable, and gives you the line's aching sense of time seen from outside. Rashi's long reading, that a divine day is a thousand human years and so Adam, who lived 930, died within it, is a rabbinic calculation and not in the text.

philological_notes.note: A watch: a division of the night during which a guard keeps watch. Metzudat Zion says it is a third of the night; Metzudat David and Meiri 'one watch of the night's watches'.

verses.translation_literal: You sweep them away; sleep they are; in the morning, like grass, it passes on.
verses.translation_dramatic: You sweep them off like a flood. They become a sleep, a dream that is gone on waking. And at dawn they are like the grass: here, and then passing on.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse is among the hardest in the psalm, and no translation is safe. 'Zeramtam' comes from zerem, the downpour or torrent (Rashi cites Habakkuk 3:10, 'a flood of waters'), so God 'floods' or 'sweeps away' people. 'Shenah' is simply 'sleep', and Radak, Metzudat David and Meiri read it as the dream that leaves nothing behind when you wake. The KJV and ASV 'as with a flood' adds a simile the Hebrew has not got; it says you flood them, flatly. Then 'yachalof' has two meanings, 'passes away' and 'sprouts renewed' (Metzudat Zion and Meiri cite Isaiah 40:31 and Job 14:7 for the second), and the KJV takes 'groweth up' where the Hebrew may equally mean 'is gone'. The image is then of grass that comes up in the morning dew and is withered by evening. Keep the ambiguity alive in performance: a flood, a dream, a blade of grass, each gone almost before it is seen.

philological_notes.note: From zerem, 'downpour, torrent': 'you flood them'. Rashi connects it to 'a flood of waters'; Metzudat Zion to the rushing of water, then 'lent to the rush of years'.
Either 'passes on' or 'is renewed' (as in 'they renew strength'). Metzudat Zion reads it as renewal; Radak and Meiri support the parallel with verse 6. The ambiguity is probably deliberate.

verses.translation_literal: In the morning it blossoms and passes on; toward evening it is cut down and dries up.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the morning it flowers, bright, green, wet with dew. By evening it is crushed and dry, and brittle in the hand.
verses.directors_commentary: One day, from sunrise to sunset, is the whole life, and the verse is built like a day: two verbs for morning, two for evening. In the Judean hills the grass flourishes after rain and the hot dry wind and sun (the sirocco) can wither it within hours; that is the concrete weather behind the image. The KJV 'in the evening it is cut down' hides a rare verb: 'yemolel' (Radak says it is a rare form, a pilel, 'to be cut down'; Meiri says it is related to melilot, ears of grain rubbed between the hands, 'so dry it crumbles'). So the grass is not scythed; it is dry enough to be rubbed to powder. The KJV also repeats 'groweth up' for 'chalaf' again, where the sense 'passes' fits both halves. Say 'dries up' as the last word, with nothing after it.

philological_notes.note: A rare form. Radak takes it as a pilel meaning 'to be cut off' and Metzudat Zion as 'cutting off'; Meiri thinks it is related to the idea of rubbing between the fingers, ears of grain made crumbly by dryness. 'Withers, is cut down' are both possible; the sense is of something brittle.

verses.translation_literal: For we are finished in your nose, and in your heat we are dismayed.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it is your anger that ends us. By your wrath we are seized with terror, and we are undone.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Af' is both 'nose' and 'anger': in Hebrew, anger shows as hard, flared breathing through the nostrils, so 'in your nose' (be'appekha) is the literal picture and the KJV 'thine anger' is the dead metaphor. 'Chemah' is 'heat, rage', a hotter word, and the verse pairs them for emphasis. The psalm now turns from general (all humans pass) to personal: 'we', with the 'for' (ki) saying that the brevity of life is not just nature but a consequence of God's anger. Radak and Metzudat David say the speaker here is the exile, 'we who are in exile'; Malbim reads two kinds of punishment, personal sin and the general death decreed on Adam. In the ancient Near East a god's anger was the standard explanation of calamity. 'Nivhalnu' is panic, not 'trouble': the KJV's 'troubled' is far too mild for a word that elsewhere describes people thrown into terror.

philological_notes.note: 'Nose', and by extension 'anger', because anger shows in the nostrils. Here with the preposition 'in': 'in your nose'.
To be terrified, to be thrown into panic (a niphal). Ibn Ezra relates it to 'bahalah', hurry and fear together.

verses.translation_literal: You have set our iniquities before you, our hidden [sins] in the light of your face.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have set our wrongdoing before you, laid out in the open. And what we kept hidden, what we thought no one had seen, stands in the full light of your face.
verses.directors_commentary: The picture is of evidence laid out on a table before a judge, and then of a lamp held up to the hidden thing. 'Neged' means 'in front of, opposite', so the sins are set where God cannot fail to see them. The light of God's face (me'or panekha) is the opposite of the common blessing 'let his face shine on you': here, the same light exposes. 'Alumenu' is rare and disputed: Rashi takes it as 'the sins of our youth' (from 'elem', a youth, cited with 1 Samuel 17:56); Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David take it from 'ta'alumah', 'a hidden thing'. The KJV 'secret sins' follows the second; the Hebrew itself is only 'our hidden things', and the word 'sins' is supplied. Radak notes the form lacks the plural yod, so it could be singular. The Ketiv and Qere of 'shatah' (written without final heh, read with it) make no difference to meaning.

philological_notes.note: Either 'our hidden [sins]' (from alam 'to hide'; Meiri, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion) or 'the sins of our youth' (Rashi, from 'elem'). Spelled without the plural yod, which Radak and Meiri discuss.
'To the light of your face'. Rashi glosses 'opposite you, so as to look at them'. The usual blessing image, the shining face, is turned here into exposure.

verses.translation_literal: For all our days have turned away in your fury; we finish our years like a sigh.
verses.translation_dramatic: All our days turn away under your wrath, and drain off. We bring our years to their end like a breath let out, a murmur, a sigh that is already gone.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Panu' is 'they turn' as the sun turns to evening: the days face away and leave. 'Evrah' is not simply 'wrath': it is anger that overflows the bank, from the root 'avar', 'cross over' (Malbim says it is anger that crosses the limit). The KJV 'we spend our years as a tale that is told' is a famous line, but it is not what the Hebrew says. 'Hegeh' is a sound with no words in it, a sigh, a groan or a murmur (the same word is used of the growl of thunder and of a quiet meditation). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all read it as speech or breath that vanishes. The KJV's choice of a 'tale' makes a life a story that has an end and an audience; the Hebrew is more bare, and more despairing. 'Kilinu' is a verb of ending, 'we finish', and Radak notes it is transitive: we bring about the end of our own years, a dark little detail.

philological_notes.note: A murmur, a sigh, a breath of sound. Rashi: 'like speech that hurries to its end'; Ibn Ezra: speech that has no standing, one moment there and then as though it never was; Metzudat Zion compares 'let my tongue murmur'. 'A tale told' (KJV) is an old tradition, not the plain sense.
'They turned' (away), as day turns into evening. Rashi: 'they turned and were consumed and went away'; Metzudat David: 'went away'.

verses.translation_literal: The days of our years, in them [are] seventy years, and if by strengths, eighty years, and their pride [is] toil and trouble, for it is cut off quickly and we fly away.
verses.translation_dramatic: The days of our years: seventy, that is the sum of them. If we are strong, eighty. And even at their best, all that swagger of theirs is toil and trouble. For it is soon cut off, and we are gone, flown away.
verses.directors_commentary: In a world where most children died young and old men were rare, seventy is the full measure and eighty a mark of unusual vigour; 'by strengths' (bigvurot) is the plural of strength, 'if the body has strength upon strength'. The text says what the old men of the ancient world knew: the years of one's prime are the hardest years. 'Rahbam' is 'their bluster, their pride' from the root 'to swagger', and the KJV 'their strength' makes it sound admirable where the Hebrew sounds almost bitter; the ASV 'pride' is truer. 'Amal va-aven' is 'toil and trouble' (aven can also mean futility or wickedness), and the KJV 'sorrow' loses the working-hard sense of 'amal'. The commentators note that Moses himself lived to a hundred and twenty, and give different solutions: Ibn Ezra suggests the psalm speaks in the voice of every generation, and Meiri that it speaks prophetically. The verse ends with a bird: 'we fly away' (na'ufah), a last, light image. 'Gaz' is 'cut off, sheared' as in shearing wool (Metzudat Zion cites Jeremiah 'cut off your hair'), so life is sheared and we fly.

philological_notes.note: 'Their pride, their bluster, their vigour'. Metzudat Zion links it to 'ירהבו' (Isaiah 3:5, 'the youth will be insolent') and takes it as strengthening; Ibn Ezra reads it as the days of youthful strength. The KJV 'strength' is a possible but weaker reading.
'To be cut off', as wool or hair is shorn. Rashi takes it as 'passing away' and cites Numbers 11:31; Metzudat Zion, 'cutting off, plucking', as in Jeremiah 7:29.
'And we fly away', from the root for flying birds. Ibn Ezra offers alternatives (a wandering bird, or 'darkness'); Radak: 'we go quickly to the grave as a bird'.

verses.translation_literal: Who [is] knowing the strength of your nose, and, as your fear, your fury?
verses.translation_dramatic: Who really knows the force of your anger? Who can measure it, or take the full weight of your wrath as it deserves to be feared?
verses.directors_commentary: The question is rhetorical and the answer is no one. 'Oz' is 'strength, force', and 'af' is again the nose, so 'the strength of your nose' is the first half's picture, a flaring blast. The second half is cryptic: 'ukhe-yir'atekha evratekha', 'and as your fear, your fury'. Rashi reads that your fury is as severe as the fear you deserve; Radak and Meiri hear Leviticus 10:3, 'among those who are near me I will be sanctified', that is, the more one fears God, the more the wrath falls on the nearest. The KJV 'even according to thy fear, so is thy wrath' picks that reading. The ASV and BBE pick others. Do not decide on stage: let the line hang as a question. The mood is not defiance but awe: a man trying to understand a power too large for him, the same man who sang of the mountains' birth.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'and as your fear, your fury'. Read variously: your wrath matches the fear owed you (Rashi, Radak), or your wrath is as hidden as your fear is (Metzudat David). The line is deliberately compressed.

verses.translation_literal: To count our days, so make known, and we shall bring a heart of wisdom.
verses.translation_dramatic: Teach us to count our days, just so. Show us how, and we will gather up a heart of wisdom.
verses.directors_commentary: After eleven verses of lament, a request, and the first in the psalm. 'Lim'not' is 'to count' as one counts coins or sheep, not 'to number' in the vague sense of the KJV; the plea is for God to teach us to do the arithmetic of a life, to see how few the days are. 'Hoda' is 'make known' (a hiphil, 'cause to know'), so the KJV 'teach' is fair, but the Hebrew is stronger: let us know it in the gut. 'Ken' means 'so, in this way', and Rashi hears a numerical pun (kaf-nun is 70). Then 'venavi' is 'and we will bring' (not 'apply', as in KJV): the heart of wisdom is something carried in from outside, a harvest brought home. Ibn Ezra compares it to the plea 'let me know my end' (Psalm 39); Metzudat David says that God's lesson will give wisdom in proportion to our few years. Do not play this as despair; it is the psalm's hinge from lament to petition.

philological_notes.note: To count, to reckon a number: not a general reflection on mortality but an arithmetic. Ibn Ezra: 'give us a heart to know how to count our days', so that we know how few they are.
'And we will bring' (hiphil). Rashi and Metzudat Zion note it is a verb of 'bringing'; the KJV 'apply' softens it. A heart of wisdom is something gathered and brought in.

verses.translation_literal: Turn back, YHWH! Until when? And relent over your servants.
verses.translation_dramatic: Turn back, LORD. Turn back to us. How long, how long must it be? Let the heat of your anger cool, and be moved to pity for the ones who serve you.
verses.directors_commentary:
After twelve verses of dust, evening grass and the seventy-year span of a life, the prayer finally turns to command. Notice the bluntness: shuvah, a plain imperative, 'turn back!', the word used of someone who has walked away. Israel's prayer treats God as having turned his face. 'Until when?' (ad matai) is the stock cry of the lament psalms (Ps 6:4; 74:10; 80:4). It is not a request for information but an accusation that has stopped waiting.

The KJV's 'let it repent thee' is the quaint part. 'Repent' in 1611 meant 'feel regret and change course', and the Hebrew verb here, nacham (Niphal), is exactly that: be sorry, relent, change your mind. Modern readers hear 'repent' as confessing sin, which makes the line sound as if God must apologise; the plea is for him to take pity and reverse the sentence. The same verb is used when Moses begs the LORD to relent from the disaster planned for the people (Exod 32:12, 14). Rashi hears the first verb as 'turn back from your burning anger' and the second as 'think a good thought for your servants'; Ibn Ezra notes that speaking of God relenting is a figure drawn from human experience. The speakers call themselves 'your servants', the language of a vassal who has nothing to bargain with but his loyalty to the master.

philological_notes.note: Niphal imperative of nacham: 'be sorry, feel compassion, change your mind'. Not 'repent' in the modern sense of confessing wrongdoing. Here it asks God to be moved from judgment to pity.
'Until when?', the fixed lament formula of the Psalter; it carries impatience, not a request for a date.

verses.translation_literal: Satisfy us in the morning [with] your covenant-loyalty, and let us shout for joy and rejoice in all our days.
verses.translation_dramatic: And when morning comes, let it come as bread to the hungry: fill us, LORD, with your faithful love, until we are full of it. Then we will cry out for joy and we will be glad, through every day we are given.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood lifts here from the night of the lament to morning. The verb sabe'a is the language of a meal: 'fill us to satiety'. The speakers are not asking for a feeling but for the kind of fullness a famished people feels after bread. What fills them is chesed, the covenant loyalty that the LORD has sworn to keep; the KJV's 'mercy' tilts it toward pardon, whereas chesed is the faithfulness that holds a relationship together. The KJV's 'early' for babboker is archaic English for 'at dawn' and hides the plain 'in the morning'.

For an ancient hearer morning is when help arrives: the night watch ends, the battle is decided at daybreak, the sacrifice is offered. Rashi reads it as the day of deliverance after the night of distress, and Radak likewise; Metzudat David and Meiri take it as 'every morning'; Ibn Ezra and Meiri also hear 'in our youth'. The two joy verbs are a pair: rannen is the loud, vocal cry of celebration, simcha the inward gladness. The KJV flattens them into 'rejoice and be glad'. The Hebrew also turns on the cohortative: 'let us shout' is the speakers' own vow, offered back once they are filled.

philological_notes.note: Piel imperative of save'a, 'be sated'; here 'make us full', the language of a meal rather than of mere comfort.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: faithfulness that keeps a bond. 'Mercy' (KJV) emphasises forgiveness more than the Hebrew does.
'In the morning': the dawn of deliverance (Rashi, Radak), each morning (Metzudat David) or youth (Meiri, Ibn Ezra).

verses.translation_literal: Make us glad according to the days [you] afflicted us, [the] years [we] saw evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: As long as you made us bow, as many seasons as we looked on trouble, so long, LORD, let us be glad.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pivot of the psalm: a request for balance. 'Make us glad' (sammechenu) answers the earlier 'we have been consumed' of the lament; the speakers ask that joy be measured out by the same ruler as pain. The Hebrew is clipped and symmetrical, two parallel clauses without 'wherein': days you afflicted us // years we saw evil. The KJV supplies 'wherein' twice and turns the compact couplet into a chain of clauses.

The verb 'afflicted' (innitanu) is the language of humbling, the same root used of the oppression in Egypt (Exod 1:11–12). Ra'ah, 'evil', is not moral wickedness but calamity, hardship; 'we have seen evil' means 'we have lived through it'. Readers have long argued about the ruler. Rashi, working from an old midrashic scheme, counts days for days, years for years, the days of the Messiah matching the years of exile. Radak rejects that arithmetic: the point is not that joy will last only as long as the suffering but that, as grief was great, so joy will be, without end. Meiri agrees: the greater the suffering, the greater the gladness to come. Ibn Ezra only notes that the afflictions were illnesses and anxieties. No ancient listener would hear a quid pro quo; they would hear a people claiming that the covenant keeps a balance.

philological_notes.note: Piel of 'anah: humble, afflict, oppress. It is the verb of the Egyptian bondage and of the fast of Yom Kippur; the afflicting is done to a person.
'Evil' as calamity or hardship, not moral wickedness.

verses.translation_literal: Let it be seen to your servants, your work, and your splendor upon their children.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them see it, your servants: let them see what your hands are doing. And let your splendor rest on their children, as a light that does not stop with us.
verses.directors_commentary:
The grammar is tilted for effect: the verb comes first (yera'eh, 'let it be seen'), then the people it is shown to, and only then the thing itself, 'your work'. The line makes the audience wait for the subject, as the speakers wait. Both nouns are God's: po'al, his 'work' (the same noun used in the Song of Moses, Deut 32:4), and hadar, 'splendor' or 'majesty', a word of royal dignity. The KJV's 'glory' is a stock word that covers several Hebrew terms (kavod, hod, hadar); here 'splendor' preserves the regal tone.

The speakers ask for something visible. God has so far been experienced as the one who afflicts; now they want to see him at work, and see it not only themselves but in the next generation, 'upon their children'. Ancient Near Eastern vassals pledged loyalty for sons as well as themselves; the covenant is inherited. Radak notes the hope that the deliverance will come in the fathers' own days, so that fathers and sons see it together. Malbim reads it as the vision of God's ongoing creative action. The KJV 'unto … their children' loses the change of preposition: 'to' (el) the servants, 'upon' (al) the children, a splendor that settles over them like a mantle.

philological_notes.note: 'Your work, your doing' (singular, despite STEPBible's 'deed[s]'); in Radak's reading the work of deliverance.
Splendor, majesty, the dignity of a king; Metzudat Zion glosses it as beauty. 'Glory' (KJV) is broader.

verses.translation_literal: And let there be [the] sweetness of [the] Lord our God upon us, and [the] work of our hands establish upon us, and [the] work of our hands establish it.
verses.translation_dramatic: And let the sweetness of the Lord our God rest on us. Whatever our hands have made, set it firm beneath us. Yes, the work of our hands, set it firm, and let it stand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on the thing everyone hears at once: the repeated line. 'The work of our hands, establish it', said twice, the second time with the pronoun 'it' added. In an oral culture repetition is not filler; it is the speakers hammering a nail. Radak says the doubling is for emphasis; Rashi finds two blessings in it, one for the Tabernacle's building and one for all labour. Ibn Ezra reads the first as the removal of obstacles in our work, the second as its completion.

No'am, here 'sweetness', is the quality of a thing that is pleasant to the taste or the ear; Metzudat Zion ties it to a verse in Proverbs 9 about bread that is pleasant. The KJV's 'beauty' narrows it to what the eye sees, and BBE's 'pleasure' leaves it unclear whether the pleasure is God's or ours. The wish is that the LORD's own pleasantness, his gracious favour, should rest on them. After seven decades of dust and 'we are consumed', the speakers ask that what they do should not vanish with them: kun means to set firm, as one sets a foundation. The hands are those of builders, farmers and weavers, the small labours of a life. The KJV's 'upon us' is literal, but the Hebrew preposition 'alenu can also be 'for us' or 'on our behalf', and the second occurrence, with the object 'it' (konnehu), makes the work itself the thing established. Malbim, a long way from the plain sense, finds in the verse a prayer for the moral and inner life; the prayer reads equally well as a plain wish for success and permanence.

philological_notes.note: Sweetness, pleasantness, graciousness; the quality of something delightful. KJV 'beauty' and ASV 'favor' choose different parts of the range.
Polel imperative of kun, 'make firm, set on a foundation'. Rashi calls it a language of supplication, like 'guard!' (Ps 25:20) and 'judge!' (Ps 82:8).
